The rate of passive diffusion is governed by the drug's ability to partition from aqueous solution into the lipid bilayer, diffuse across it, and re-partition into the aqueous phase on the other side. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) provides the driving force for membrane partitioning. Molecular weight < 500 Da. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design. Compact, low-flexibility conformations reduce the entropic cost of membrane insertion.

Charged species at the assay pH (typically pH 7.4) — carboxylates, phosphates, quaternary amines — have very poor passive diffusion because the charge cannot be buried in the lipid interior. Very hydrophilic molecules (logP < 0) lack the driving force for membrane partitioning. High molecular weight (>600 Da) and many rotatable bonds (>10) also reduce permeability.
